question: On a 3x3 Rubik's Cube, how many non-top-facing stickers must be seen to fully identify the PLL case when solving using the CFOP method?

1.text:
In CFOP the U face is already one colour after OLL so the whole of the
Last Layer permutation lives in the side colours of the U layer pieces.
On the U layer there are

* 4 U edges, each with one non-U sticker, and
* 4 U corners, each with two non-U stickers,

i.e. 4+8=12 non-U stickers belong to the U layer.  The permutation of the
four edges and the permutation of the four corners is all that is needed
for a PLL name.

In a normal look you read one side sticker per U piece.  That is the four
U edge side stickers and one side sticker, the front sticker in the usual
facing, for each of the four U corners, 4+4 = 8 non-U stickers which are
the ones that are actually inspected by a speed-solver.  The fourth edge
and the fourth corner are forced by the parity of a permutation, so that
in the information theoretic sense seven non-U stickers already carry the
21 different PLL names, the classic “eight sticker’’ look being the
practical implementation of that.  Formally the U layer has 12 non-U
stickers, 8 of which are normally read, 7 of which are information
theoretically necessary. ∎

5.text:
In CFOP the last step is a pure U–layer permutation.  After an OLL the
U face is monochrome

* U = U

so the colour information that is left on the U–layer is the colour that
is on the four F,R,B,L faces of the eight U–layer cubies.  Up to a
global rotation the abstract PLL is the cyclic type of the four U corners
and the four U edges.  Colour wise you therefore have to be able to
refer each of the eight U–layer cubies to a reference colour.  One
non–U sticker per U–layer cubie is enough to give the reference.

* 4 U–corners × 1 visible side sticker per corner = 4
* 4 U–edges  × 1 visible side sticker per edge   = 4

i.e. eight distinct non–U stickers, one per U–layer piece, is the
information-theoretic minimum.  In the strict geometric description of
the U–layer that is

4 corners × 2 side stickers + 4 edges × 1 side sticker = 12

non–U stickers, eight of them on the four corners and four on the four
edges, that belong to the U–layer.  Of course once you have a reference
for the abstract permutation the case is already determined up to
rotation, so in the usual abstract sense the pattern of the eight
U–layer pieces can be read on the monochrome U face itself, i.e. with
no side information at all.  The twelve side stickers are what is
normally quoted as the “U–layer side” that has to be inspected in
practice, eight distinct ones being the information theoretic minimum.

3.text:
In CFOP the U face is oriented by OLL so that

* U - U = yellow / white on the whole U face

and the PLL is the permutation of the seven U layer cubies.  The
orientation of the U layer is now fixed, so the only information that
is left in the U layer lives on the stickers that are not on U.

The U layer contains

* 4 U edges : U - F , U - R , U - B , U - L : 1 non-U sticker each
* 4 U corners : UFR , UFL , UBL , UBR : 2 non-U stickers each

so that, apart from the four side centres, the whole information
content of the U slice is

4×1 + 4×2 = 12

non-U stickers, i.e. the 12 stickers of the top ring

UFRf, UFRr, UFLf, UFLl, UBLb, UBLl, UBRb, UBRr
Uf, Ur, Ub, Ul

The U face itself is now monochromatic and carries no PLL
information.  That is the U ring that is normally spoken of as ‘the
PLL pattern’.  In the worst case you have to be able to read the whole
U ring, 12 side stickers, to know exactly which of the 21 PLL
permutations you are looking at.  In practice the 21 cases are far
more redundant than 12 stickers and a normal human recognition uses a
very small subset of the ring, typically the four U edge side stickers
and the four U corner side stickers that are visible on the front/
right view, i.e. a 6-8 sticker view, and information-theoretically
about log2 21≈4.4 bit ≈ 3–5 stickers are enough to separate the 21
cases.  The 12 sticker U ring is the textbook ‘you have to be able to
read the whole top layer’ statement.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8

After OLL the U face is monochromatic so the top-facing stickers carry no information about permutation. The PLL is the permutation of the 4 U-layer edges and the 4 U-layer corners, and after OLL each of those eight pieces can be distinguished only by its non-U side colour.

In practice you need at least one side sticker from every U-layer piece to read the permutation unambiguously. The four U edges each contribute a single visible non-top sticker on the front/back/left/right face of the U layer, and each of the four U corners contributes at least one visible non-top sticker on its side face. That is 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-top-facing stickers. Seeing fewer than one sticker per piece leaves a symmetry or a mirror ambiguity between two PLL classes, so eight non-U stickers is the minimal guaranteed set needed to identify the case.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 4 non-top-facing stickers are enough to uniquely pin down the PLL case in CFOP.

After OLL the U face is monochromatic, so the only information left for the last layer is the permutation of the 8 U-layer pieces. The up sticker of each piece is already known, so each piece is identified by the single side sticker that is visible on the 4 side faces. Because a valid cube must have even permutation parity between the corners and the edges, the corner permutation is forced once the edge permutation is known, and vice-versa.

In practice you can resolve the whole U-layer permutation by reading the four side stickers of the U edges — or equivalently the four side stickers of the U corners — and the remaining four side stickers are then determined by parity and the U-face pattern you are already seeing. Two mirror pairs that look identical on the U face are separated by the relative orientation of just one corner and one edge, so four well-chosen side stickers, e.g. the four edge side stickers, already break all ambiguities among the 21 PLL cases.

12.text:
In CFOP the U face is monochromatic after an OLL.  The U face itself
therefore carries no information about the permutation.  The information
that distinguishes one PLL from another is carried by the side of the
U–slice.

The U–slice is made of

* 4 U–edges.  Each U–edge shows one sticker on a side face, 4 stickers,
* 4 U–corners.  Each U–corner shows two stickers on side faces, 8
stickers.

i.e. 12 non–U stickers belong to the U–slice, 4+8 =12 in all, 8 distinct
U–layer pieces.  Once the U face is known to be solved you never have to
look at the U stickers again, the whole PLL is read off the side of the
U slice.

In practice the two stickers of a corner are redundant for a
permutation reading and you can read a U–corner by its one front/left/
right/back sticker.  It is therefore conventional to speak of the eight
U–layer pieces, four edge stickers and four corner stickers, that have
to be read around the top, 12 stickers if you count the two side
stickers of each corner.  With a conventional inspection you can in fact
recognise any of the 21 PLL classes from a convenient 6–8 sticker
sub–set of that U–slice, the 12 stickers being the information–theoretic
upper bound for the U–slice.

10.text:
In CFOP the U layer is solved for orientation. What is left on the U slice
is the permutation of the four U edges and the four U corners. Up to a U
rotation there are

* 4 U edges  $4\times 1=4$  non-U stickers,
* 4 U corners $4\times 2=8$  non-U stickers

on the U slice, i.e. 12 side stickers in all.  The  F  R  B L  colours of
those 12 stickers are the whole data that carries the permutation.

In particular an edge is carried by the single side sticker that sits on
the face it is on and a corner is carried by the two side stickers that
sit on the two side faces it is on.  Up to the four-fold rotational
symmetry of the U face the permutation of the eight U pieces is fixed by
$n-1$ independent pieces, i.e. by seven independent U pieces.  In the
usual “look from the top’’ inspection this is realised by the 4 edge
side stickers and one identifying side sticker for each of four corners,
the eight side stickers which are visible round the U perimeter, the
other four corner stickers being the complement of the eight.  That is
the 12-sticker information of the U slice, 7 independent pieces in the
usual information theoretic sense, which is what is normally quoted as
the 8-side-sticker PLL look.  The 9 U stickers are all the same colour
after OLL and therefore carry no permutation information.

6.text:
In CFOP the OLL step is assumed to be done, i.e. the U face is a
monochrome face.  The U face itself therefore carries no information
about the permutation.  What is left to recognise is the permutation
of the eight U cubies,

* 4 U edges, each of which is identified on the U layer by the single
side sticker which is not on U, and
* 4 U corners, each of which is identified on the U layer by the
two side stickers which are not on U.

Hence the whole information content of the last layer is contained in
the side data of the U layer.  There are

* $4{\rm\;edges}\times 1=4$ edge side stickers, and
* $4{\rm\;corners}\times 2=8$ corner side stickers,

i.e. $4+8=12$ non-U stickers belonging to the U layer, the eight U
cubies.  That is the information which has to be inspected in order to
know in which of the 21 PLL classes the last layer lies.  In
particular, once the eight U cubies are known the fourth cubie of each
type is forced by the conservation of the set of side colours, so that
in the non-redundant sense the permutation is fixed by the seven
independent side stickers, the usual way of saying that the case is
fixed by the eight U cubies, i.e. by the four U-edges and the four
U-corners, often quoted as the eight non-U stickers of the U layer –
the twelve side stickers, eight independent ones, of the U layer.  This
is the $4\times 1+4\times 2$ side data which is normally spoken of as
the “seven/eight sticker” PLL recognition. ∎

2.text:
In CFOP the last layer is oriented before it is permuted, so after OLL the
U face is a solid colour.  The U stickers themselves therefore carry no
information about the permutation.  The permutation is the side colours
that belong to the eight cubies that are on the U layer.

There are eight U–layer cubies,

* 4 U corners, each with 2 non–U side stickers,
* 4 U edges, each with 1 non–U side sticker,

i.e. $4\times2+4\times1=12$ U-layer side stickers.  In information
theoretic terms the eight cubies are the objects you have to distinguish.
Four corners determine the fourth corner and three edges determine the
fourth edge by parity, so seven distinct side stickers are already
information theoretically enough to pin the 21 PLL classes down and in
practice the case is read off the eight U-layer pieces.  That is the
twelve U–layer side stickers, eight distinct pieces, which is what is
normally quoted as “the four corners and the four edges’’ of the top
layer.  If the pieces are counted, eight pieces have to be read, seven
of which are information-theoretically redundant. ∎

4.text:
In CFOP the OLL is finished, so the whole U face is monochrome.  The
U layer is then

* 4 U–edges.  An U–edge has one side facelet left on the four side
faces.  The colour that you see on the side face tells you which edge
cubie is in that position;
* 4 U–corners.  An U–corner has two side facelets left on the four side
faces.  One side facelet per corner is enough to say which corner cubie
is in that position.

Hence there are eight distinguishable U–layer cubies to be named.  That
is eight informative side facelets in the U–layer.  In the cube the
U–layer carries

* 4 edges × 1 side facelet = 4
* 4 corners × 2 side facelets = 8

i.e. 12 non–U facelets in total, the 8 informative facelets being a
subset of those 12.  In practice the 12 side facelets of the U layer are
inspected, and up to rotation the information can be reduced to seven
independent facelets, the familiar “one facelet per cubie’’ 8-facelet
recognition.  This is the 12 facelets, 8 independent, that are
normally quoted for a full PLL recognition.

8.text:
In CFOP the U face is already a single colour after OLL so the whole
information which is left in the last layer is the permutation of the
four U-corners and the four U-edges.  With the U colour known a U–
edge is completely identified by the one side colour that it shows on
the four side faces

* UF – the sticker of the front-up edge on F,
* UR – the sticker of the right-up edge on R,
* UB – the sticker of the back-up edge on B,
* UL – the sticker of the left-up edge on L,

and a U–corner is completely identified by the two side colours that
it shows.  On the four side faces you therefore see

* 4 U-edges × 1 side sticker per edge = 4 stickers,
* 4 U-corners × 2 side stickers per corner = 8 stickers,

i.e. the 12 non-U stickers that belong to the U-layer.  That is the
12 side stickers of the last layer that are in principle needed to know
which of the 8 last-layer pieces is in which of the 8 last-layer
positions.  It is normally phrased as the eight last-layer pieces, four
edges + four corners, the 12 side stickers being 4+8.  Up to the
obvious parity and rotational redundancy the information is 7
independent stickers, which is why in practice a PLL is recognised from
the 4 edge and 4 corner side colours, the familiar 8-piece, 12-sticker,
U-layer view. ∎

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: 8 non-top stickers. In CFOP the U layer at PLL is solved for orientation, so the 8 pieces sitting on top are 4 edges and 4 corners. The U sticker tells you the colour that is on top, but it does not by itself tell you which physical piece is occupying each U position. To resolve the permutation you need at least one identifying side colour for each of those 8 pieces. That is one side sticker per edge, 4 stickers, and one side sticker per corner, 4 stickers, for a total of 8 non-U stickers in addition to the 8 U stickers you are already looking at. With the U face pattern plus those 8 side identifiers the corner cycle and edge cycle are uniquely determined and the PLL case is fixed.

11.text:
In CFOP the last layer is first oriented and the U–layer is then
solved up to permutation.  After OLL the orientation of every U–layer
piece is fixed, so a U–layer piece is completely identified by the
colour that it shows on U.  There are four different U–edge pieces and
four different U–corner pieces and every one of them has a unique U
colour, e.g.

* the U–corner which shows W on U is always the W–R–B corner,
* the U–edge which shows W on U is always the W–R edge,
etc.

Hence the map

position on U  ↔  U-colour of the piece which occupies the position

is a bijection.  The position of each of the four U–edges and of each
of the four U–corners, i.e. the whole permutation of the 8 U–layer
pieces, is therefore already written on the 9 stickers of U.  In
particular the 21 essentially different PLL permutations are already
distinguished by the pattern that they make on U up to a rotation about
the U axis.  The side colours of the U–layer pieces are then forced by
the piece that the U–colour identifies, so in the strict information
theoretic sense no sticker which is not on U is needed to know which
of the 21 PLL classes you are in.  The U–face alone is a complete
encoding of the last–layer permutation.

Up to the usual practical caveat that the solver has to fix the
orientation of the cube in space, the orientation is fixed by the U
pattern itself and, e.g., the familiar ``headlights’’ are just a
convenient way of reading the U pattern on the front of the cube.  The
limiting practical reading is therefore one or two front side stickers
to fix the absolute front of the cube, often quoted as the two adjacent
side stickers that give the headlights.  In the idealised information
theoretic statement this is zero non-U stickers.

9.text:
In CFOP the U face is already solved for OLL so the U face is
monochrome.  Up to a whole–cube rotation the whole PLL information is
contained in the ring of side stickers which belong to the U layer.

The U layer contains 4 U edges and 4 U corners

* a U edge is completely identified by its one side colour, the U
colour being known;
* a U corner is completely identified by its two side colours, the U
colour being known.

Hence the U ring is made up of

* 4×1 = 4 side stickers on the four U edges
* 4×2 = 8 side stickers on the four U corners

i.e. 12 non–U stickers in all, 8 piece-identifiers.  Parity of the
cube makes the eighth piece redundant so that seven independent
non–U stickers, i.e. in ordinary language eight distinct piece
identifiers, four edge stickers and one side sticker per corner, are
information theoretically enough to fix the permutation of the U
layer and therefore the PLL case.  In practice the whole U ring is
read, 4 edge side stickers + 8 corner side stickers, the 9 up stickers
being useless after OLL.  This is usually quoted as the eight
distinguishing stickers of the U ring, 7 independent up to parity, and
12 physical non-U stickers if both corner stickers are counted.

15.text:
In CFOP the last layer is arrived at with the U face oriented.  After the
OLL is done the nine U stickers are all the same colour and carry no
information about a permutation.  The only thing that is still unknown on
the last layer is the permutation of the four U edges and the four U
corners.  On the U layer

* an U edge has one U sticker and one side sticker,
* an U corner has one U sticker and two side stickers,

so that the U layer has in all

$4\times1+4\times2 =12$

stickers which are not on U.  Those are the four side stickers of the
four U edges and the eight side stickers of the four U corners,
three per side face.

Up to the four AUF rotations the permutation of the last layer is fixed
by the cyclic order of the four edge side colours and by the cyclic order
of the four corner side colours.  Parity ties the edge and the corner
permutations together so that once the four edge side stickers are known
only three independent corner side stickers are needed to fix the whole
U-layer permutation.  In ordinary language this is quoted as the four
edge side stickers $E_{i}$ and one side sticker of each of the four
U corners $C_{i}$, i.e. the eight side stickers of the U layer, and with
the parity redundancy this can be reduced to the four $E_{i}$ plus three
independent $C_{i}$ – seven distinct non-U stickers – which is enough to
distinguish the 21 PLL classes.  Counting the whole side pattern of
the U layer the layer possesses twelve non-U stickers, four edge side
stickers $+ 8$ corner side stickers, and that is the information which is
normally inspected to name the PLL case.  This is the eight-sticker
form usually quoted in practice, seven independent stickers in the
parity-reduced form.

In CFOP the last layer is oriented before it is permuted, so after OLL the
U face is a solid colour.  The U stickers themselves therefore carry no
information about the permutation.  The permutation is the side colours
that belong to the eight cubies that are on the U layer.

There are eight U–layer cubies,

* 4 U corners, each with 2 non–U side stickers,
* 4 U edges, each with 1 non–U side sticker,

i.e. $4\times2+4\times1=12$ U-layer side stickers.  In information
theoretic terms the eight cubies are the objects you have to distinguish.
Four corners determine the fourth corner and three edges determine the
fourth edge by parity, so seven distinct side stickers are already
information theoretically enough to pin the 21 PLL classes down and in
practice the case is read off the eight U-layer pieces.  That is the
twelve U–layer side stickers, eight distinct pieces, which is what is
normally quoted as “the four corners and the four edges’’ of the top
layer.  If the pieces are counted, eight pieces have to be read, seven
of which are information-theoretically redundant. ∎
public_text.4:
In CFOP the OLL is finished, so the whole U face is monochrome.  The
U layer is then

* 4 U–edges.  An U–edge has one side facelet left on the four side
faces.  The colour that you see on the side face tells you which edge
cubie is in that position;
* 4 U–corners.  An U–corner has two side facelets left on the four side
faces.  One side facelet per corner is enough to say which corner cubie
is in that position.

Hence there are eight distinguishable U–layer cubies to be named.  That
is eight informative side facelets in the U–layer.  In the cube the
U–layer carries

* 4 edges × 1 side facelet = 4
* 4 corners × 2 side facelets = 8

i.e. 12 non–U facelets in total, the 8 informative facelets being a
subset of those 12.  In practice the 12 side facelets of the U layer are
inspected, and up to rotation the information can be reduced to seven
independent facelets, the familiar “one facelet per cubie’’ 8-facelet
recognition.  This is the 12 facelets, 8 independent, that are
normally quoted for a full PLL recognition.
public_text.8:
In CFOP the U face is already a single colour after OLL so the whole
information which is left in the last layer is the permutation of the
four U-corners and the four U-edges.  With the U colour known a U–
edge is completely identified by the one side colour that it shows on
the four side faces

* UF – the sticker of the front-up edge on F,
* UR – the sticker of the right-up edge on R,
* UB – the sticker of the back-up edge on B,
* UL – the sticker of the left-up edge on L,

and a U–corner is completely identified by the two side colours that
it shows.  On the four side faces you therefore see

* 4 U-edges × 1 side sticker per edge = 4 stickers,
* 4 U-corners × 2 side stickers per corner = 8 stickers,

i.e. the 12 non-U stickers that belong to the U-layer.  That is the
12 side stickers of the last layer that are in principle needed to know
which of the 8 last-layer pieces is in which of the 8 last-layer
positions.  It is normally phrased as the eight last-layer pieces, four
edges + four corners, the 12 side stickers being 4+8.  Up to the
obvious parity and rotational redundancy the information is 7
independent stickers, which is why in practice a PLL is recognised from
the 4 edge and 4 corner side colours, the familiar 8-piece, 12-sticker,
U-layer view. ∎
public_text.13: 8 non-top stickers. In CFOP the U layer at PLL is solved for orientation, so the 8 pieces sitting on top are 4 edges and 4 corners. The U sticker tells you the colour that is on top, but it does not by itself tell you which physical piece is occupying each U position. To resolve the permutation you need at least one identifying side colour for each of those 8 pieces. That is one side sticker per edge, 4 stickers, and one side sticker per corner, 4 stickers, for a total of 8 non-U stickers in addition to the 8 U stickers you are already looking at. With the U face pattern plus those 8 side identifiers the corner cycle and edge cycle are uniquely determined and the PLL case is fixed.
public_text.11:
In CFOP the last layer is first oriented and the U–layer is then
solved up to permutation.  After OLL the orientation of every U–layer
piece is fixed, so a U–layer piece is completely identified by the
colour that it shows on U.  There are four different U–edge pieces and
four different U–corner pieces and every one of them has a unique U
colour, e.g.

* the U–corner which shows W on U is always the W–R–B corner,
* the U–edge which shows W on U is always the W–R edge,
etc.

Hence the map

position on U  ↔  U-colour of the piece which occupies the position

is a bijection.  The position of each of the four U–edges and of each
of the four U–corners, i.e. the whole permutation of the 8 U–layer
pieces, is therefore already written on the 9 stickers of U.  In
particular the 21 essentially different PLL permutations are already
distinguished by the pattern that they make on U up to a rotation about
the U axis.  The side colours of the U–layer pieces are then forced by
the piece that the U–colour identifies, so in the strict information
theoretic sense no sticker which is not on U is needed to know which
of the 21 PLL classes you are in.  The U–face alone is a complete
encoding of the last–layer permutation.

Up to the usual practical caveat that the solver has to fix the
orientation of the cube in space, the orientation is fixed by the U
pattern itself and, e.g., the familiar ``headlights’’ are just a
convenient way of reading the U pattern on the front of the cube.  The
limiting practical reading is therefore one or two front side stickers
to fix the absolute front of the cube, often quoted as the two adjacent
side stickers that give the headlights.  In the idealised information
theoretic statement this is zero non-U stickers.
public_text.9:
In CFOP the U face is already solved for OLL so the U face is
monochrome.  Up to a whole–cube rotation the whole PLL information is
contained in the ring of side stickers which belong to the U layer.

The U layer contains 4 U edges and 4 U corners

* a U edge is completely identified by its one side colour, the U
colour being known;
* a U corner is completely identified by its two side colours, the U
colour being known.

Hence the U ring is made up of

* 4×1 = 4 side stickers on the four U edges
* 4×2 = 8 side stickers on the four U corners

i.e. 12 non–U stickers in all, 8 piece-identifiers.  Parity of the
cube makes the eighth piece redundant so that seven independent
non–U stickers, i.e. in ordinary language eight distinct piece
identifiers, four edge stickers and one side sticker per corner, are
information theoretically enough to fix the permutation of the U
layer and therefore the PLL case.  In practice the whole U ring is
read, 4 edge side stickers + 8 corner side stickers, the 9 up stickers
being useless after OLL.  This is usually quoted as the eight
distinguishing stickers of the U ring, 7 independent up to parity, and
12 physical non-U stickers if both corner stickers are counted.
public_text.15:
In CFOP the last layer is arrived at with the U face oriented.  After the
OLL is done the nine U stickers are all the same colour and carry no
information about a permutation.  The only thing that is still unknown on
the last layer is the permutation of the four U edges and the four U
corners.  On the U layer

* an U edge has one U sticker and one side sticker,
* an U corner has one U sticker and two side stickers,

so that the U layer has in all

$4\times1+4\times2 =12$

stickers which are not on U.  Those are the four side stickers of the
four U edges and the eight side stickers of the four U corners,
three per side face.

Up to the four AUF rotations the permutation of the last layer is fixed
by the cyclic order of the four edge side colours and by the cyclic order
of the four corner side colours.  Parity ties the edge and the corner
permutations together so that once the four edge side stickers are known
only three independent corner side stickers are needed to fix the whole
U-layer permutation.  In ordinary language this is quoted as the four
edge side stickers $E_{i}$ and one side sticker of each of the four
U corners $C_{i}$, i.e. the eight side stickers of the U layer, and with
the parity redundancy this can be reduced to the four $E_{i}$ plus three
independent $C_{i}$ – seven distinct non-U stickers – which is enough to
distinguish the 21 PLL classes.  Counting the whole side pattern of
the U layer the layer possesses twelve non-U stickers, four edge side
stickers $+ 8$ corner side stickers, and that is the information which is
normally inspected to name the PLL case.  This is the eight-sticker
form usually quoted in practice, seven independent stickers in the
parity-reduced form.

9.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion converges on the structure of the U-slice after OLL in CFOP.

After OLL the U face is monochrome and carries no permutation information. The only remaining data is the permutation of the eight U-layer cubies. The U-slice physically contains

* 4 U-edges × 1 side sticker = 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U-corners × 2 side stickers = 8 non-U stickers

i.e. 4 + 8 = 12 non-U stickers that belong to the U layer. That is the textbook “U ring’’.

In practice the permutation is read piece by piece. One identifying side colour per U-layer piece is enough to name the piece in its U position, so in ordinary inspection

* 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-U stickers

are the ones that are actually looked at around the top perimeter. The fourth edge and the fourth corner are forced by parity of a cube permutation, so information-theoretically seven independent non-U stickers, the familiar eight-sticker look, distinguish the 21 essentially different PLL classes. Up to the four-fold AUF the eight piece identifiers are the conventional practical reading; the full physical inventory of the U slice is the 12 side stickers.

The claim that zero non-U stickers are needed because the U pattern encodes the permutation is incorrect under OLL: the U face is a solid colour after OLL so the U stickers themselves do not distinguish the eight U cubies. The “four stickers are enough’’ parity argument is an information-theoretic lower bound that ignores the need for an unambiguous piece-by-piece identification in the worst case. Unresolved is whether the question wants the physical inventory 12, the practical 8-per-piece reading, or the parity-reduced 7 independent stickers; the bulk of the colleagues quote the 12-sticker U ring and the 8-sticker practical recognition.

reflection_text.9:
The discussion converges on the structure of the U-slice after OLL in CFOP.

After OLL the U face is monochrome and carries no permutation information. The only remaining data is the permutation of the eight U-layer cubies. The U-slice physically contains

* 4 U-edges × 1 side sticker = 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U-corners × 2 side stickers = 8 non-U stickers

i.e. 4 + 8 = 12 non-U stickers that belong to the U layer. That is the textbook “U ring’’.

In practice the permutation is read piece by piece. One identifying side colour per U-layer piece is enough to name the piece in its U position, so in ordinary inspection

* 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-U stickers

are the ones that are actually looked at around the top perimeter. The fourth edge and the fourth corner are forced by parity of a cube permutation, so information-theoretically seven independent non-U stickers, the familiar eight-sticker look, distinguish the 21 essentially different PLL classes. Up to the four-fold AUF the eight piece identifiers are the conventional practical reading; the full physical inventory of the U slice is the 12 side stickers.

The claim that zero non-U stickers are needed because the U pattern encodes the permutation is incorrect under OLL: the U face is a solid colour after OLL so the U stickers themselves do not distinguish the eight U cubies. The “four stickers are enough’’ parity argument is an information-theoretic lower bound that ignores the need for an unambiguous piece-by-piece identification in the worst case. Unresolved is whether the question wants the physical inventory 12, the practical 8-per-piece reading, or the parity-reduced 7 independent stickers; the bulk of the colleagues quote the 12-sticker U ring and the 8-sticker practical recognition.
reflection_text.2:
The deliberation is split between the geometric inventory of the U slice and the information-theoretic minimum needed for a PLL name.

After OLL the U face is monochrome, so the U stickers carry no permutation information. The permutation lives on the U slice.

* Inventory: 4 U edges × 1 side sticker = 4, 4 U corners × 2 side stickers = 8, i.e. 12 non-U stickers belong to the U layer. This is the 12-sticker U ring that is normally quoted as the whole last-layer side data. Colleagues 1,2,3,4,6,8,10,12,15 all give this 4+8=12 count.

* Practical reading: one identifying side sticker per U cubie is normally used. That is 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-U stickers that are inspected around the top, the familiar “eight sticker” PLL look. Several colleagues 4,5,7,13 quote this 8-piece view. With parity of a cube the fourth edge and the fourth corner are forced, so the information-theoretic independent count is 7 stickers, log2 21≈4.4 bit, which is why 7 independent non-U stickers are enough to separate the 21 PLL classes. 

The zero-sticker claim of colleague 11 is inconsistent with CFOP: after OLL the U face is solid colour, so the U colour is the same for all four white corners / four white edges and does not identify which physical piece occupies a given U position. The side colours are required. The 4-sticker claim of colleague 14 is optimistic; one side sticker per corner alone leaves a front/right ambiguity because a white corner is defined by its two side colours.

Current best synthesis: the U layer geometrically possesses 12 non-top stickers, 4 edge + 8 corner. In ordinary recognition 8 distinct non-U stickers, one per cubie, are read, i.e. 7 independent up to parity, the 12-sticker ring being the full upper bound. That is the consensus 12-total / 8-practical / 7-independent statement repeated across the majority of colleagues.
reflection_text.15:
The round-0 discussion is sharply split on how the PLL information is counted.

* The U layer after OLL is monochromatic on U. The only permutation data lives on the side of the U slice.
* Geometry of the slice: 4 U edges × 1 side sticker =4, 4 U corners ×2 side stickers=8. 4+8=12 non-U facelets belong to the U layer, i.e. 8 U-cubies. That is the textbook “U-ring’’ count used by Colleagues 1,2,3,4,6,8,10,12,15.
* Practical reading: one identifying side sticker per cubie is enough. 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers =8 distinct non-U stickers are normally inspected around the top perimeter. This is the familiar 8-sticker PLL look. Colleagues 7,13,5,4,6,8 etc. quote this.
* Parity/redundancy: the fourth edge and the fourth corner are forced by parity / by the set of colours already seen. Information-theoretically the 21 PLL classes need log2 21≈4.4 bits, i.e. ~7 independent non-U stickers. The 8-sticker look is 7 independent up to rotation/parity. Colleagues 1,2,10,15,2 note 7 independent, 8 practical.
* Outlier claims: Colleague 11 argues zero non-U stickers are needed because the U-face pattern encodes the permutation. That is false in CFOP: after OLL the U face is monochrome, so its 9 stickers carry no permutation information. The U colour is the same for all eight U-cubies, so the map position↔U-colour is not injective. The side colours are required.
* Colleague 14’s “4 stickers are enough’’ is an over-minimisation. Four edge side stickers alone do not resolve corner mirror ambiguities without at least three independent corner identifiers; the usual minimal guaranteed set is the eight piece identifiers, seven independent.
* Unresolved nuance: whether the question asks for total physical non-U facelets on the U slice, 12, or for the minimal guaranteed identifying set, 8 piece identifiers, 7 independent. The consensus practical answer is 8 non-U stickers, one per U-cubie, which correspond to the 12 physical side facelets of the U layer, 7 of them information-theoretically independent.

The discussion therefore supports 12 side facelets on the U layer in principle, 8 distinct identifiers in ordinary practice, 7 independent information-theoretically. Colleague 11’s zero-sticker claim is inconsistent with the monochrome U face after OLL.

4.text:
After OLL the U face is monochrome, so the 9 U stickers carry no
permutation information.  All of the PLL information is in the side
data of the eight U-layer cubies that sit on the U slice.

* 4 U-edges : 1 side sticker per edge, 4×1 = 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U-corners : 2 side stickers per corner, 4×2 = 8 non-U stickers

Hence the U-ring physically contains 4+8 = 12 non-U stickers.  Up to a
U rotation the permutation of the last layer is the cyclic order of the
four U edges and the four U corners.  One identifying side colour per
U-layer piece is enough to name the piece, i.e. one side sticker per
edge and one side sticker per corner.

In normal inspection that is

4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-U
stickers, one per U-layer cubie,

the familiar eight-sticker PLL look.  The 12 side stickers of the U
ring are the 4 edge stickers + the 8 corner stickers, the eighth piece
being forced by parity so that seven independent non-U stickers,
log2 21≈4.4 bit, are information-theoretically enough to distinguish the
21 PLL classes.  The 9 U stickers are useless after OLL. ∎

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: After OLL the U face is monochrome and therefore carries no permutation information. The PLL is the permutation of the eight U-layer pieces, four U edges and four U corners, up to a U rotation.

A U edge is identified on the U layer by its single side sticker, UF, UR, UB, UL. A U corner is identified on the U layer by its two side stickers, but one side sticker per corner is enough to tell which corner cubie is in that U position once the U colour is known. That is the usual “one identifier per cubie’’ reading.

Hence in a guaranteed worst-case inspection you need

* 4 U edges × 1 side sticker = 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U corners × 1 identifying side sticker = 4 non-U stickers

= 8 distinct non-U stickers, one per U-layer piece, in addition to the monochrome U face you are already looking at.

The U layer physically has 4×1+4×2 =12 side stickers, and up to parity and the four-fold U rotation the information is 7 independent. That is the information-theoretic lower bound that is often quoted. It is not a guaranteed inspection bound: you cannot know in advance which of the eight piece identifiers is the redundant one, and with only 6 or 7 arbitrarily chosen side stickers you can leave mirror/rotation ambiguities between e.g. U and U’, Z and S, or T vs. its mirror. 

In practice speed-solvers read the eight side identifiers around the U perimeter, four edge side stickers and one side sticker per corner, i.e. the familiar eight-sticker look. That is the minimal set that identifies the PLL case without having to assume piece identity from U colour alone or assume you have happened to pick the lucky redundant sticker. The twelve side stickers are the physical upper bound; the eight piece-identifiers are the practical guaranteed minimum.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The PLL is the permutation of the eight U-layer cubies after OLL, so the U face itself is useless for the permutation – it is mono-colour. What remains is side information on the U ring.

There are four U edges and four U corners on top. With the U colour known, an edge is identified by the single side sticker it shows on F/R/B/L, and a corner is identified by at least one of its two side stickers. To name the permutation in absolute space, i.e. with a fixed front and AUF resolved, you need a reference for every U-layer piece.

That is 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-U identifiers. The U layer physically contains 4×1+4×2 = 12 non-U stickers, the other four corner stickers being the complements of the eight identifiers. Parity makes the eighth piece redundant in the information-theoretic sense, so seven independent stickers carry the 21 PLL classes, but you cannot guarantee a priori which seven you will see.

Colleague 11’s idealised zero-sticker claim assumes identification up to rotation of the whole cube. In practice a solver must fix AUF and distinguish mirror cases. The familiar headlights / block / etc. recognition is a front-referenced reading, and that reference is supplied by side stickers. Four edge stickers alone, as suggested by Colleague 14, leaves mirror ambiguities for the corners, and reading the U pattern alone does not fix the absolute front.

The conventional and guaranteed practical read is therefore the eight piece identifiers: one side sticker per U edge and one side sticker per U corner around the top. In terms of physical stickers that is the 12-sticker U ring, quoted in practice as the eight-sticker PLL look, seven independent up to parity.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: After OLL the U face is monochrome so the nine U stickers carry no PLL information. What remains is the permutation of the eight U-layer pieces.

The U-layer physically owns

* 4 U-edges × 1 side sticker = 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U-corners × 2 side stickers = 8 non-U stickers

i.e. 12 non-U stickers on the U-slice. In a normal inspection we do not need both side stickers of a corner, one identifying side sticker per piece is enough to name the piece because the U colour is already known.

That is one side sticker for each of the four U-edges and one side sticker for each of the four U-corners: 4+4 = 8 distinct non-top identifiers, the familiar 8-sticker look around the U perimeter. The other four corner side stickers are the complement of those eight.

The seven-independent-sticker information-theoretic bound is real, but it is a bound, not a guaranteed recognition. With only six non-U stickers you are missing at least two of the eight U-layer pieces. Parity ties corners to edges but it does not resolve local mirror/swap ambiguities between the unobserved pieces: two different PLL classes can agree on any six well-chosen side stickers and differ only on the two you have not looked at. The zero-sticker ideal of Colleague 11 and the four-sticker claim of Colleague 14 rely on being able to infer the missing pieces from the U pattern and parity alone, which in practice requires fixing the absolute orientation of the cube and still leaves an ambiguous mirror pair for a human look. 

The textbook, guaranteed recognition is the one-per-piece read: the four edge side stickers plus one side sticker per corner, eight non-top stickers, twelve physical non-U stickers on the U slice. That is the set that unambiguously fixes the corner cycle and the edge cycle and therefore the PLL name.

6.text:
In CFOP the PLL is taken with the U face oriented by OLL.  The nine U
stickers are then monochrome and carry no permutation information.  All
of the permutation information of the last layer is carried by the side
data of the eight U layer cubies.

* 4 U edges : U – side. 1 non-U sticker per edge,
  4 × 1 = 4 non-U stickers;
* 4 U corners : U – side – side. 2 non-U stickers per corner,
  4 × 2 = 8 non-U stickers.

Hence the U ring that is normally inspected for PLL is

4 edge side stickers + 8 corner side stickers = 12

non-U stickers belonging to the U slice, i.e. the 12 side stickers of the
top ring UFRf, UFRr, UFLf, UFLl, UBLb, UBLl, UBRb, UBRr, Uf, Ur, Ub, Ul.
The nine U stickers are useless for permutation after OLL.

In ordinary human recognition the two side stickers of a corner are
redundant for the permutation and the case is read off one identifying
side sticker per U cubie, 4 edge + 4 corner = 8 distinct non-U stickers,
the familiar eight-sticker PLL look.  Up to the parity coupling of
corners and edges the eight pieces are 7 information-theoretically
independent, log2 21 ≈ 4.4 bit, which is why the eight-sticker, twelve-
sticker geometric description is normally quoted as the eight piece,
twelve sticker U-ring inspection. ∎

information theoretic independent content of the 21 PLL classes is

public_text.7:
After OLL the U face is monochrome and therefore carries no permutation information. The PLL is the permutation of the eight U-layer pieces, four U edges and four U corners, up to a U rotation.

A U edge is identified on the U layer by its single side sticker, UF, UR, UB, UL. A U corner is identified on the U layer by its two side stickers, but one side sticker per corner is enough to tell which corner cubie is in that U position once the U colour is known. That is the usual “one identifier per cubie’’ reading.

Hence in a guaranteed worst-case inspection you need

* 4 U edges × 1 side sticker = 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U corners × 1 identifying side sticker = 4 non-U stickers

= 8 distinct non-U stickers, one per U-layer piece, in addition to the monochrome U face you are already looking at.

The U layer physically has 4×1+4×2 =12 side stickers, and up to parity and the four-fold U rotation the information is 7 independent. That is the information-theoretic lower bound that is often quoted. It is not a guaranteed inspection bound: you cannot know in advance which of the eight piece identifiers is the redundant one, and with only 6 or 7 arbitrarily chosen side stickers you can leave mirror/rotation ambiguities between e.g. U and U’, Z and S, or T vs. its mirror. 

In practice speed-solvers read the eight side identifiers around the U perimeter, four edge side stickers and one side sticker per corner, i.e. the familiar eight-sticker look. That is the minimal set that identifies the PLL case without having to assume piece identity from U colour alone or assume you have happened to pick the lucky redundant sticker. The twelve side stickers are the physical upper bound; the eight piece-identifiers are the practical guaranteed minimum.
public_text.14:
The PLL is the permutation of the eight U-layer cubies after OLL, so the U face itself is useless for the permutation – it is mono-colour. What remains is side information on the U ring.

There are four U edges and four U corners on top. With the U colour known, an edge is identified by the single side sticker it shows on F/R/B/L, and a corner is identified by at least one of its two side stickers. To name the permutation in absolute space, i.e. with a fixed front and AUF resolved, you need a reference for every U-layer piece.

That is 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-U identifiers. The U layer physically contains 4×1+4×2 = 12 non-U stickers, the other four corner stickers being the complements of the eight identifiers. Parity makes the eighth piece redundant in the information-theoretic sense, so seven independent stickers carry the 21 PLL classes, but you cannot guarantee a priori which seven you will see.

Colleague 11’s idealised zero-sticker claim assumes identification up to rotation of the whole cube. In practice a solver must fix AUF and distinguish mirror cases. The familiar headlights / block / etc. recognition is a front-referenced reading, and that reference is supplied by side stickers. Four edge stickers alone, as suggested by Colleague 14, leaves mirror ambiguities for the corners, and reading the U pattern alone does not fix the absolute front.

The conventional and guaranteed practical read is therefore the eight piece identifiers: one side sticker per U edge and one side sticker per U corner around the top. In terms of physical stickers that is the 12-sticker U ring, quoted in practice as the eight-sticker PLL look, seven independent up to parity.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: After OLL the U face is monochrome, the nine U stickers carry no permutation information at all. The PLL is the permutation of the eight U-layer cubies up to AUF.

The U slice physically owns

* 4 U-edges × 1 side sticker = 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U-corners × 2 side stickers = 8 non-U stickers

i.e. 12 non-U stickers on the U ring. The U colour is known so a U edge is identified by its single side colour and a U corner is identified by at least one of its two side colours.

For a guaranteed, front-referenced recognition you need an identifying side colour for every U-layer piece. That is one side sticker per U edge and one side sticker per U corner:

4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-top identifiers,

the familiar one-per-cubie 8-sticker look round the U perimeter. The other four corner side stickers are the complement of that set.

The 7 independent sticker information-theoretic bound is real for the 21 PLL classes, log2 21 ≈ 4.4 bit, and the eighth piece is forced by parity up to AUF. It is a bound on average information content, not a guaranteed inspection. You cannot know in advance which of the eight piece identifiers will be the redundant one, and with only six or seven arbitrarily chosen side stickers you leave at least two U-layer pieces unobserved.

Parity ties corners to edges but it does not resolve local mirror/swap ambiguities with an incomplete observation: U versus U’, Z versus S, T versus its mirror, etc., remain indistinguishable if you have not seen a fixed front-referenced identifier for each of the eight pieces. Six non-U stickers means you are missing at least two of the eight U-layer pieces entirely, and no amount of parity or U-colour knowledge can disambiguate those mirror pairs in the worst case.

That is why the textbook, guaranteed practical read is the one-per-piece read: eight distinct non-top stickers, four edge side stickers and one side sticker per corner, i.e. the 12-sticker U ring quoted in practice as the eight-sticker, seven-independent PLL recognition.

The U slice physically owns

* 4 U-edges × 1 side sticker = 4 non-U stickers

the familiar one-per-cubie 8-sticker look round the U perimeter. The other four corner side stickers are the complement of that set.

The 7 independent sticker information-theoretic bound is real for the 21 PLL classes, log2 21 ≈ 4.4 bit, and the eighth piece is forced by parity up to AUF. It is a bound on average information content, not a guaranteed inspection. You cannot know in advance which of the eight piece identifiers will be the redundant one, and with only six or seven arbitrarily chosen side stickers you leave at least two U-layer pieces unobserved.

Parity ties corners to edges but it does not resolve local mirror/swap ambiguities with an incomplete observation: U versus U’, Z versus S, T versus its mirror, etc., remain indistinguishable if you have not seen a fixed front-referenced identifier for each of the eight pieces. Six non-U stickers means you are missing at least two of the eight U-layer pieces entirely, and no amount of parity or U-colour knowledge can disambiguate those mirror pairs in the worst case.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: After OLL the U face is monochrome so the nine U stickers carry zero permutation information. The PLL is the permutation of the eight U-layer cubies up to AUF, and the whole of that information lives on the U ring.

The U slice physically owns
* 4 U edges × 1 side sticker = 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U corners × 2 side stickers = 8 non-U stickers
for a total of 12 non-U facelets UF, UR, UB, UL and UFRf,UFRr,UFLf,UFLl,UBLb,UBLl,UBRb,UBRr. The nine U stickers are useless for the permutation.

With the U colour known a U edge is named by its single side colour and a U corner is named by its side colours. One identifying side sticker per U cubie is enough to name the cubie in its U position. In a front-referenced, AUF-resolved inspection that is the normal operational read:

4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-top identifiers, one per U-layer piece, the familiar eight-sticker look round the top perimeter. The other four corner side stickers are the complement of those eight, giving the 12 physical side stickers of the U ring.

The 7 independent, log2 21 ≈ 4.4 bit information-theoretic bound is correct as an average information content, and up to four-fold AUF and corner/edge parity the eighth piece is forced. It is a bound, not a guaranteed inspection set. You cannot know a priori which of the eight piece identifiers will be the redundant one, and with only six arbitrarily chosen non-U stickers you are missing at least two of the eight U-layer pieces entirely.

Parity ties corners to edges but it does not resolve local mirror / swap ambiguities with an incomplete front-referenced observation: U versus U′, Z versus S, T versus its mirror, etc., remain indistinguishable if you have not seen a fixed front-referenced identifier for each of the eight pieces. Six non-U stickers leaves at least two U-layer pieces unobserved and no amount of parity or U-colour knowledge can disambiguate those mirror pairs in the worst case.

That is why the textbook guaranteed practical read is the one-per-piece read: eight distinct non-top stickers, four edge side stickers and one side sticker per corner, i.e. the 12-sticker U ring conventionally quoted as the eight-sticker, seven-independent PLL recognition. ∎

public_text.7:
After OLL the U face is monochrome so the nine U stickers carry zero permutation information. The PLL is the permutation of the eight U-layer cubies up to AUF, and the whole of that information lives on the U ring.

The U slice physically owns
* 4 U edges × 1 side sticker = 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U corners × 2 side stickers = 8 non-U stickers
for a total of 12 non-U facelets UF, UR, UB, UL and UFRf,UFRr,UFLf,UFLl,UBLb,UBLl,UBRb,UBRr. The nine U stickers are useless for the permutation.

With the U colour known a U edge is named by its single side colour and a U corner is named by its side colours. One identifying side sticker per U cubie is enough to name the cubie in its U position. In a front-referenced, AUF-resolved inspection that is the normal operational read:

4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct non-top identifiers, one per U-layer piece, the familiar eight-sticker look round the top perimeter. The other four corner side stickers are the complement of those eight, giving the 12 physical side stickers of the U ring.

The 7 independent, log2 21 ≈ 4.4 bit information-theoretic bound is correct as an average information content, and up to four-fold AUF and corner/edge parity the eighth piece is forced. It is a bound, not a guaranteed inspection set. You cannot know a priori which of the eight piece identifiers will be the redundant one, and with only six arbitrarily chosen non-U stickers you are missing at least two of the eight U-layer pieces entirely.

Parity ties corners to edges but it does not resolve local mirror / swap ambiguities with an incomplete front-referenced observation: U versus U′, Z versus S, T versus its mirror, etc., remain indistinguishable if you have not seen a fixed front-referenced identifier for each of the eight pieces. Six non-U stickers leaves at least two U-layer pieces unobserved and no amount of parity or U-colour knowledge can disambiguate those mirror pairs in the worst case.

That is why the textbook guaranteed practical read is the one-per-piece read: eight distinct non-top stickers, four edge side stickers and one side sticker per corner, i.e. the 12-sticker U ring conventionally quoted as the eight-sticker, seven-independent PLL recognition. ∎

After OLL the U face is monochrome so the nine U stickers carry no permutation information. The PLL is the permutation of the eight U-layer cubies, four U edges and four U corners, up to four-fold AUF.

That information lives entirely on the U ring.

* 4 U edges : 1 side sticker per edge = 4 non-U facelets UF,UR,UB,UL
* 4 U corners : 2 side stickers per corner = 8 non-U facelets UFRf,UFRr,UFLf,UFLl,UBLb,UBLl,UBRb,UBRr

4+8 = 12 non-U facelets physically belong to the U slice. The nine U stickers are useless for permutation after OLL.

With the U colour known a U edge is named by its single side colour and a U corner is named by its two side colours. One identifying side colour per U-layer cubie is enough to name the cubie in its U position. In ordinary front-referenced, AUF-resolved inspection that is the operational one-per-piece read:

The other four corner side stickers are the complement of those eight, i.e. the 12-sticker U ring quoted above.
